description: An interdisciplinary team of university engineers about to graduate: five systems engineers and one statistician from Escuela Colombiana de Ingeniería Julio Garavito University and Pontificia Universidad Javeriana (Colombia). We turn raw data into clear, working products, blending full-stack, cloud, AI and rigorous statistics. Global top-45 finalists in 2025, we're back for more. Fast communicators, early shippers, fans of hard problems.
summary:
NISAR Hazard Watch is a radar evidence explorer built for "Dancing with the SARs" NASA challenge. Pick a place on a 3D globe and the app reads real NISAR L-band radar scenes from NASA's ASF archive, measures whether the echo there changed beyond that place's own normal range, and draws the result as map layers and measured values. Radar sees through clouds and at night, so floods, wildfires, vegetation loss, landslides and earthquakes can be examined when optical images fail. For earthquake areas it maps interferometric coherence and phase.

A fresh area answers in roughly one to two and a half minutes, and measured cases such as the Chenab flood in Pakistan open at once. Where a second, independent satellite exists, the app cross-checks against it.

We kept the science honest. Results are diagnostic evidence, not validated classifiers: every value is labelled "ONLINE" or "OFFLINE", each answer lists its limitations, and the app reports no forecasts, probabilities, causes or ground displacement. A guided story, the Nova assistant, a CSV export and a printable report help non-experts understand and share what the radar shows.

Built with React and CesiumJS on Vercel, FastAPI and PostgreSQL on Railway, and parallel Python radar workers on Modal.
details:
EARTH, WITHOUT THE CLOUDS

After a flood, a fire or an earthquake, the sky is usually the last thing to clear. Optical satellites photograph the clouds, not the ground, and the people who need answers have to wait. NASA-ISRO's NISAR radar does not wait: it carries its own light, so it sees through cloud and at night.We built NISAR Hazard Watch to turn that radar into something anyone can read.

PICK A PLACE, GET AN ANSWER

Open the globe and pick a place. Our backend finds the NISAR passes that cover it, a worker streams only the pixels it needs from NASA's ASF archive, and in about one to two and a half minutes the globe shows what the radar measured: whether the echo there changed beyond that place's own normal range.

Calm water bounces radar away, so flooded ground turns dark. Our guided story follows the Chenab flood in Pakistan in six chapters, from the question to the evidence, and checks the radar against an independent optical reference from NASA OPERA.

EVIDENCE YOU CAN OPEN

Every answer unfolds into a sheet that shows how it was computed, the measured figures, the sources and the quality of the data.

HONEST BY DESIGN

Radar shows change, not cause. So the app says plainly what it cannot tell: no forecasts, no probabilities, no hectares, no validated ground displacement. Results are diagnostic evidence, every value is labelled Real or Demo, and each answer lists its limitations.

BEYOND FLOODS

The same pipeline looks at wildfires (with NASA FIRMS fire detections as context), vegetation loss, landslides and earthquakes, where it maps interferometric coherence and phase. Nova, an assistant powered by Claude, explains each result in plain words from the measured numbers, and any result can be exported as a CSV or a printable report.

UNDER THE HOOD

React and CesiumJS on Vercel; a FastAPI and PostgreSQL backend on Railway; and Python radar workers on Modal that read many scenes at once and can run dozens of analyses in parallel.

WHO WE ARE

Six students from Escuela Colombiana de Ingeniería Julio Garavito University and Pontificia Universidad Javeriana, in Colombia, who built the app, the API and the models in parallel.

SI DISCLOSURE

We used Claude (Anthropic), through Claude Code, to help write code, tests, documentation and the diagrams, and Nova's answers are generated live by Claude. The radar data, the measurements and the scientific decisions come from NASA data and from our team.
